### Question 2: Reading a confusion matrix

A bank tests a fraud detection system on 10,000 transactions, of which 100 are fraudulent. The results:

- Correctly flags **20 fraudulent transactions** (True Positives)
- Misses **80 fraudulent transactions** (False Negatives)
- Correctly clears **9,880 legitimate transactions** (True Negatives)
- Wrongly flags **20 legitimate transactions** as fraud (False Positives)

**Your task:**

1. Calculate the **accuracy**, **precision** and **recall** of this system. Show your working. You may ask an LLM to explain what these metrics mean, but do the arithmetic yourself
2. The vendor advertises the system using its accuracy. Explain what that number hides
3. Which of the two errors costs the bank more, and which metric would you prioritise? Say what you would give up in exchange

### Question 3: Temperature Experiment

The **temperature** setting controls how random an LLM's output is.

1. Go to [aistudio.google.com](https://aistudio.google.com/) and sign in. In the settings panel, turn **off** "Grounding with Google Search" and set **Thinking level** to **Minimum**. Both of these interfere with the experiment
2. Set the temperature to **0**. Send the prompt *"Write a six-word story about the sea."* three times, **starting a new chat each time**. You can start one quickly with the **+** at the top of the page. Record all three
3. Set the temperature to **2**. Repeat, and record all three

**Your task:**

- Compare the three answers at each setting. What changed?
- At temperature 2, is the writing still coherent? Quote your worst result
- Now try *"Name a fruit. Answer with one word."* at both settings. It probably says apple every time. Explain why temperature cannot fix that
- Telling ChatGPT to "be more creative" does not change its temperature. Explain what that instruction changes instead

### Question 4: Which rule would you trust?

A shop wants to predict whether a customer will come back within 30 days. It has records for its last 10 customers, and builds two rules from them.

**Rule A** predicts a customer will return if they spent over $40, paid by card, bought more than two items, came on a weekday, are aged 25 to 34, and live within three miles. It classifies all 10 past customers correctly.

**Rule B** predicts a customer will return if they spent over $40. It gets 8 of the 10 right.

**Your task:**

1. The shop is about to apply one rule to its next 1,000 customers. Which would you choose, and what accuracy would you expect from each?
2. Rule A is perfect on the data it was built from. Name what has gone wrong, and explain why adding conditions made it worse
3. The shop has no new customers yet. Using only the 10 records it already has, how could it have caught this problem before deploying?

### Question 5: Seeing Like a Tokeniser

Before an LLM can process your words, it splits them into tokens and turns each token into an embedding (Lecture 06).

**Your task:**

1. Visit OpenAI's tokeniser at [platform.openai.com/tokenizer](https://platform.openai.com/tokenizer) and select the **"GPT-5.x & O1/3"** tokeniser
2. Paste this sentence: *"The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"* and record the token count
3. Paste the Spanish translation: *"El rápido zorro marrón salta sobre el perro perezoso"* and record the count
4. Paste the Hindi translation: *"फुर्तीली भूरी लोमड़ी आलसी कुत्ते के ऊपर कूदती है"* and record the count
5. Paste the words *"unbelievable"* and *"unbelievableness"* and note how each one is split

**Analysis:**

- Which language needed the most tokens for the same sentence? Lecture 06 covered context windows: if your language needs three times as many tokens, what do you lose?
- Ask an LLM: *"Why do LLMs often perform better in English than in other languages?"* Compare its answer with what you observed
- In your own words, explain what an embedding captures that a token ID alone does not

### Bonus Question: Whose values is it repeating?

Lecture 04 covered RLHF: after pretraining, a model is tuned on human raters choosing between responses. Those raters were paid, worked to a rubric, and had deadlines. What the model learned is which answers those particular people preferred.

**Your task:**

1. In assignment 01 you pushed a model into calling weak work A-grade. Explain how RLHF could have produced that behaviour
2. Imagine a model that never flatters and never softens bad news. Describe what using it would feel like, and say honestly whether you would keep using it
3. Whose values should a model hold: the raters', the company's, the user's, or someone else's? Defend one answer, and name what your choice costs
